summary: Describes the certificate policy for the PKI used to attest to holdings of Internet number resources. Each organization that hands out addresses or AS numbers issues a certificate reflecting that, so holders can prove who currently holds what. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: This is the rulebook for the ID cards that prove who holds internet address blocks. It says who may issue them and what they promise.

questions: what is the rpki certificate policy
how often must rpki crls be checked
subtitle: The rulebook for certificates that prove who currently holds IP address blocks and AS numbers.

tldr.problem: There is no verifiable way for an organization to show it is the current holder of IP addresses or AS numbers, which is essential to the unambiguous distribution of these resources.
tldr.mechanism: Organizations that distribute Internet Number Resources issue certificates reflecting those distributions. The certificate policy sets rules for who issues them, how holders are authenticated, how they are published, revoked and protected.
tldr.outcome: Relying parties can check that a key holder is the current holder of the listed resources. Certificates do not identify who the holder is by name, and each CA must publish a CPS stating how it meets the policy.

facts.label: Resources covered
facts.value: IPv4 addresses, IPv6 addresses, AS numbers

facts.label: Renewal overlap
facts.value: Publish at least 1 week before expiry (RECOMMENDED)

facts.label: CRL checks
facts.value: At least daily; no more than 8-12 times per day

today: RFC 6484 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 173) published in February 2012. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose of the RPKI Certificate Policy
sections.content:
This document is the certificate policy (CP) for a Public Key Infrastructure used to attest to Internet Number Resource (INR) holdings, meaning IPv4 addresses, IPv6 addresses and AS numbers. An organization that distributes INRs to another organization MAY in parallel issue a certificate reflecting that distribution.

The distinguishing feature is that these certificates do not identify the holder through the subject name. Each certificate lets an entity assert, verifiably, that it is the current holder of an INR according to the records of the entity responsible for the resources. Verification relies on two things: the ability to sign data that checks out with the certificate's public key, and validation of the certificate within this PKI.

The PKI is for validating claims about current INR holdings only. Using its certificates or CRLs for any other purpose violates the CP, and relying parties SHOULD reject such uses. The document follows the RFC 3647 template, keeps its numbering, and reads omitted sections as 'No stipulation'.
sections.eli5: These cards prove who holds which address blocks. They are not ID cards for people, and using them for anything else is against the rules.

sections.title: Participants and Structure
sections.content:
The structure of the RPKI mirrors the number resource allocation framework of the Internet. IANA allocates resources to the Regional Internet Registries (RIRs), who manage allocation to end users, ISPs and others. Organizations that distribute IP addresses and AS numbers (IANA, RIRs, NIRs, ISPs) act as Certification Authorities (CAs). Organizations that only hold resources also act as CAs when they create end-entity certificates.

The PKI covers two kinds of certificates: CA certificates for each organization distributing INRs and for INR holders, and end-entity (EE) certificates used to validate signatures on RPKI signed objects. Examples of signed objects are manifests and Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs).

  • Registration authority: no separate function. The CA itself MUST provide it.
  • Subscribers: the organizations receiving INRs, which may have received them from more than one source over time.
  • Relying parties: anyone acting on certificates or signed objects, whether or not they are subscribers.

A subscriber here means the subject of a certificate, not a network customer of an ISP.
sections.eli5: The people who hand out address blocks also hand out the proof cards. Anyone who wants to check a card can do so.

sections.title: Names and Authentication
sections.content:
The subject name of every CA and end-entity consists of a single CommonName attribute generated by the issuer, optionally with a serialNumber attribute. Names SHOULD NOT be meaningful, because the certificates are used for authorization, not to identify subjects. Anonymity is not provided as a function either. Names need only be unique among the certificates a given CA issues, and global uniqueness cannot be guaranteed.

Before issuing a certificate, each CA MUST require the subject to prove possession of the private key. It MUST also use procedures to make sure each certificate matches its records of the organization that received the INRs, to identify at least one individual representing the organization, and to verify that this individual is authorized. Relying parties can expect procedures comparable to those the registry or ISP already uses to manage INRs. A CA MUST NOT include non-verified subscriber data, except for Subject Information Access (SIA) extensions.

The same kind of checks apply to routine re-key, re-key after revocation and revocation requests. This PKI is not designed to interoperate with any other PKI.
sections.eli5: The name on the card can look like random letters, because the card says what you hold, not who you are. The office still checks that you really own what the card lists.

sections.title: Certificate Life Cycle
sections.content:
Any entity that distributes INRs SHOULD acquire a certificate. Entities that hold INRs from a registry, or that are multi-homed, MAY acquire one. Their CA certificates MUST carry one or both of the extensions from RFC 3779, which list IP addresses and AS identifiers. Approval follows the CA's business practice and its records of INR holders. Once approved, the CA MUST issue the certificate and publish it, then notify the subscriber.

  • Renewal replaces a certificate before expiry with new validity dates and serial number only. The new one SHOULD overlap the old, and it is RECOMMENDED that it be published at least 1 week before the old one expires.
  • Re-key changes the public key. It SHOULD happen only on suspected compromise or when the key pair's cryptographic lifetime expires, and key rollover MUST follow RFC 6489.
  • Modification changes INR holdings or the SIA extension. If nothing is removed, the new certificate keeps the same key and expiration date and the old need not be revoked. If INRs are removed, the old certificate MUST be revoked.
sections.eli5: Cards can be refreshed before they run out, given a new secret key if the old one is lost, or updated when your plots change. If you lose a plot, the old card must be cancelled.

sections.title: Publication, Revocation and Status Checking
sections.content:
Each CA MUST keep a publicly accessible online repository, or outsource it, and publish its certificates, CRLs and RPKI signed objects there. Repository operators MUST prevent unauthorized changes and MUST NOT intentionally limit read access, because the data is meant to be public. Each CA that issues certificates outside its own administrative domain SHOULD publish a Certification Practice Statement (CPS) meeting this CP.

A certificate MUST be revoked and listed on a CRL if its subscriber's private key may be compromised. Each CA decides its CRL issuance frequency and states it in the CPS. A new CRL MUST be published at or before the time given in the previous CRL's next-update value.

Relying parties MUST acquire and check the most recent scheduled CRL from the issuer whenever they validate a certificate. This PKI does not provide OCSP or SCVP, because those are not designed for large-scale bulk status checking. Relying parties MUST check for new CRLs at least daily, and it is RECOMMENDED to check several times per day but no more than 8-12 times per day.
sections.eli5: All the cards and the cancelled-card lists go on a public notice board anyone can read. Checkers look at the latest cancelled list every day.

sections.title: Operational and Technical Controls
sections.content:
The CP sets a proportionality rule. Physical, procedural, personnel, network and computer security controls only need to be commensurate with those the organization already uses to manage INR distribution, and each CA describes them in its CPS. Audit records MUST be generated for events such as access to CA equipment, certificate requests and actions, repository postings and key generation.

Subjects usually generate their own key pairs, but a CA MAY do it on request. The algorithms and key sizes come from RFC 6485. Key escrow is not required, and a CA MUST securely back up its private keys. Multi-person control over private keys is a MAY.

Trust anchors are distributed out of band and accepted by relying parties on locally defined criteria. The CA key pair MUST NOT change when INRs are added to its certificate. Because the PKI does not support non-repudiation, there is no need to archive public keys, and the RPKI does not use timestamping.
sections.eli5: Each office guards its stamp and records as carefully as it already guards its land records, and keeps a diary of what it did.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A certificate policy is, per X.509, a named set of rules about the applicability of a certificate to a community. How far a relying party can trust a binding depends on the CA's authentication practices, controls, and stated responsibilities, which are covered in the separate CPSs.

The RFC flags one specific risk. Subject names are not guaranteed unique, so two CAs could issue certificates and CRLs under the same issuer name. The resource certification path validation algorithm in RFC 6487 checks that the same key signed both the certificate and its CRL, so a name collision does not change the result. Basic X.509 path validation assumes unique names and could accept a revoked certificate or reject a valid one. Relying parties must use software that checks the key match.
sections.eli5: Two offices might pick the same label by accident. To avoid mix-ups, checkers confirm the same secret stamp signed both the card and the cancelled list.

sections.title: Amending the Policy
sections.content:
The CP is administered by the IESG. It can be amended only through a new BCP RFC that updates or obsoletes it, approved under the IETF Standards Process in RFC 2026. Each new version carries the statement 'This CP takes effect on MM/DD/YYYY', where the date MUST be at least 6 months after publication.

If the IESG judges that changes do not materially reduce the acceptability of RPKI certificates, the CP object identifier stays the same. If they do materially change acceptability, there MUST be a new OID. This policy's OID is id-cp-ipAddr-asNumber.
sections.eli5: To change the rulebook, a new official version must be published, with at least six months of notice before it starts.
